title: Army Survival Manual Principles for City Emergencies
source: U.S. military survival manual FM 21-76-1 (public domain) / CDC
summary: Key ideas from the U.S. military survival manuals, adapted for families stuck in a town or city when power, water, and phones fail: a calm mindset, water already in your home, staying safe and low-key, signaling for help, and finding your way without GPS.

steps.title: Use the SURVIVAL checklist to stay calm
steps.body: The military survival manuals open with a memory aid that works just as well in a blackout as in the woods. S - Size up the situation, your surroundings, your health, and your gear. U - Use all your senses; slow down and notice. R - Remember where you are and where help is. V - Vanquish fear and panic by giving yourself a task. I - Improvise and improve with what you have. V - Value living; decide you will get through this. A - Act like the natives, meaning do what experienced locals do. L - Live by your wits. When stress spikes, walk through the letters out loud. It turns panic into a to-do list.

steps.title: Find the water already in your home
steps.body: CDC lists safe backup water inside the house: the tank of your water heater (the one that feeds your faucets, not a radiator boiler in older homes), melted ice made from clean water, liquid in canned fruits and vegetables, and water in the toilet tank if it is clear and has no chemical cleaner. Never drink from the toilet bowl. Pool and spa water is for washing, not drinking. Water touched by fuel or chemicals cannot be made safe. Turn off the water heater's power or gas before draining it, and let it cool. Treat outdoor water before drinking, and follow local boil-water notices.

steps.title: Stay put safely if your home is sound
steps.body: If officials have not ordered an evacuation and your home is not damaged, staying home usually beats wandering a city. Lock doors and windows, keep a way out clear in case of fire, and choose one room to gather the family at night. Cook and heat only with devices made for indoor use; never use grills, camp stoves, or generators inside, in a garage, or near windows, because carbon monoxide kills quickly. Run a battery-powered CO alarm. Keep a low profile: do not advertise supplies, and keep lights and noise modest after dark (see sec-006).

steps.title: Act like the natives - blend in
steps.body: In a city emergency, 'act like the natives' means behave like your calm, sensible neighbors. Dress plainly, carry supplies in an ordinary bag, keep cash and gear out of sight, and move with purpose. Avoid crowds that are growing angry, demonstrations, and long lines after dark. Travel in small groups and tell someone where you are going and when you will be back. Blending in reduces the chance that anyone sees you as a target; see sec-007 for more.

steps.title: Signal for help so rescuers can see you
steps.body: The manuals stress making signals as large and high-contrast as possible. From a roof, balcony, or yard, spread a bright sheet, tarp, or signal panel, or write SOS or HELP in big letters with tape or paint. Three of anything - three whistle blasts, three flashes, three bright objects in a row - is a widely understood distress signal. A mirror or shiny CD can flash sunlight toward aircraft. At night, use a flashlight or phone light in bursts. Do not burn tires or trash for smoke; the fumes are toxic and fires spread in cities.

steps.title: Find your way without GPS
steps.body: Keep a paper street map of your town in your go bag with key places marked: hospitals, fire stations, shelters, and family meeting spots. Download offline maps on your phone before trouble starts. Learn how your city numbers streets and addresses, since numbers usually climb as you move away from a central line. Count blocks as you walk and note big landmarks such as water towers, rivers, and highways. The sun rises roughly in the east and sets roughly in the west. If you are lost, stop, check your map, and ask first responders or shelter staff.

warnings: Military manuals were written for service members in combat and remote areas. Use the survival ideas, not the military tactics, and follow civilian law and official instructions.
Never use fuel-burning stoves, grills, or generators indoors or in a garage. Carbon monoxide is odorless and deadly.
Do not drink floodwater or water that smells of fuel or chemicals - it cannot be made safe at home.
Do not enter damaged buildings; they can collapse or have gas leaks.
proTips: Fill bathtubs and clean containers as soon as a storm or outage is forecast, so you are not relying on the water heater.
Tape a bright cloth panel and a whistle inside your go bag; together they weigh almost nothing.
Practice the SURVIVAL checklist on small problems, like a flat tire, so it comes easily under stress.
Mark your paper map with two routes to each meeting place.

whenNotTo: If officials order an evacuation or your home is damaged, leave instead of staying put - see sec-003.
Do not try to signal by starting fires in a city.

quickGlance.situation: You are in a town or city when power, water, and phone service fail and help may be slow.
immediate: Walk through the SURVIVAL checklist to calm down and size things up
Use safe in-home water: water heater tank, clean ice, clear toilet tank (never the bowl)
Stay put if your home is sound; never use grills or generators indoors
then: Signal for help with large bright panels, SOS, or three of anything
Navigate with a paper map and landmarks; ask responders if lost
